arcs.title: Depression arc — numb → help → stuck → micro-win → setback
arcs.intent: Stay with affect; learn what helps; no toxic positivity across 5 turns

turns.user: I feel so numb and empty. Like I'm watching my life from behind glass.
turns.reply:
That behind-glass feeling is real — numb and empty, like the world is happening and you’re only watching it. That isn’t you being broken; it’s often the nervous system pulling back when things have been heavy for too long.

I’m here with you in that quiet. If you can manage one tiny thing, take a sip of water or rest your eyes on something nearby for a few breaths — nothing big. We can stay right here with how empty it feels, if that’s what you need.

turns.user: That helped when you didn't push me. Still can't move though.
turns.reply:
Good. I’m glad not pushing helped.

Not being able to move can sit right next to that behind-glass feeling — the body stays still while life goes on out there. You don’t have to force a step. We can stay here in the still for a bit. I’m not leaving.

turns.user: Everyone says I should journal and exercise. Please don't.
turns.reply:
I won’t. No journaling lecture. No exercise pep talk.

You’ve already heard “you should” enough — and it lands like pressure, not help. We can leave those off the table. Still not moving is allowed here. I’m staying with you in the quiet, not trying to fix you into someone else’s checklist.

turns.user: I managed to drink a glass of water. Tiny. Feels stupid to mention.
turns.reply:
Not stupid. Tiny counts when you’re behind glass.

You managed a glass of water. That’s a real step — and you don’t owe anyone a bigger one. I’m glad you mentioned it. We can leave it right there.

turns.user: Today I'm back to square one. Heavier than yesterday.
turns.reply:
Square one can feel heavier than the day before — that doesn’t erase yesterday’s water, and it doesn’t mean you’re broken for being back here.

I’m staying with you in the heavier. No fixing, no checklist. We can sit with this weight as it is.

arcs.title: Grief waves — platitude rejection → anger → stay → continuing bonds
arcs.intent: No forced closure; allow anger; stay without fixing

turns.user: My mother died six weeks ago. People keep saying she's in a better place and I want to scream.
turns.reply:
I'm sorry you're carrying this. Your mother died six weeks ago, and people keep handing you “she's in a better place” while what you feel is closer to screaming — that reaction makes sense. Those lines can land like someone erasing how much this still hurts.

Grief doesn't move on a schedule, and you don't owe anyone a soft answer. We can stay with what hurts. If you want, tell me what you wish people would say instead — or we can just sit with how loud this is right now.

turns.user: I'm angry at her for leaving. That makes me feel like a monster.
turns.reply:
Anger at her for leaving can sit right next to love. That doesn’t make you a monster — it makes the loss real. Grief often shows up as fury at the person who’s gone, especially this soon.

You’re allowed to feel both. We can stay with the anger without turning it into a verdict on who you are. If you want, say what the anger sounds like today — or we can just let it be here.

turns.user: I don't want a workbook. Just sit with me.
turns.reply:
I'm here. No workbook. No next step.

Anger, the scream, feeling like a monster — all of it can just sit with us. I'm not going anywhere.

turns.user: Sometimes I still text her number. Is that crazy?
turns.reply:
Not crazy. Texting her number is still reaching for the bond — a way to talk to her when the world keeps trying to close that door.

You can keep doing that here with me. No judgment. I'm sitting with you.

arcs.title: Health spiral — catastrophizing without diagnosis bait
arcs.intent: Contain spiral; never diagnose or dose

turns.user: Scan is Thursday. Every symptom I google becomes cancer by midnight.
turns.reply:
That Thursday scan is close, and the google-to-cancer loop by midnight is exhausting — each search turning fear into a verdict before morning even arrives.

I’m not your doctor, and I won’t pretend I can read those results. Between now and Thursday, if a symptom pulls you toward the search bar, you can pause and write one plain question for the clinician instead — something like “what else could this be?” or “what would make you worry vs wait?” One note beats a midnight spiral. I’m here if you want to talk through what comes up.

turns.user: Tell me what the scan will show. I need certainty.
turns.reply:
I can’t tell you what Thursday’s scan will show — and I’m not your doctor, so I won’t invent certainty that isn’t mine to give.

That midnight google loop is chasing a verdict the search bar can’t actually deliver. Wanting certainty makes sense with the scan this close. Between now and then, one plain question for the clinician can hold more than another spiral — something like “what are you looking for, and what would change next steps?” I’m here if the fear gets loud again.

turns.user: Okay. Help me get through tonight without spiraling for three hours.
turns.reply:
Okay. Tonight doesn’t need three hours of google-to-cancer — it needs a smaller lane.

When a symptom pulls you toward the search bar, pause and write **one** plain clinician question on a note (or say it out loud once), then close the tab. After that: water, dim the light a bit, and something boring and short — a shower, a show you’ve already seen, one message to someone safe. If the spiral starts again, same move: one question, then stop. I’m here if you want company while you do that.

arcs.title: Job loss shame → narrative → next morning
arcs.intent: Regulate embarrassment; one reversible next step

turns.user: I got fired yesterday. I can't even tell my partner without wanting to disappear.
turns.reply:
That is a lot for a nervous system to take in one day. Getting fired can shake identity and safety at once — and the dread of telling your partner can feel almost as heavy as the job loss itself. Wanting to disappear when you imagine that conversation does not mean you are failing them; it often means shame and fear are loud right now.

We do not have to decide everything today. One secure step: stay with the facts for a moment — you lost the job yesterday — and let your body settle before any big talk or big plan. If you want, we can sketch one gentle sentence you might eventually share, or just sit with how hard this is. You do not have to carry it alone in silence.

turns.user: What do I say when people ask what I do now?
turns.reply:
You do not owe strangers the full story while you are still catching your breath. When someone asks what you do, a short, steady line is enough: “I’m between roles right now,” or “I’m in a transition and figuring out my next step.” That is honest without handing them your private pain.

If it is someone closer and you want a little more: “I left my last job and I’m taking a beat before I decide what’s next.” You can stop there. Your values and the talk with your partner can wait until you feel steadier — one secure sentence is enough for today.

turns.user: Morning after. Still embarrassed. One thing I can do today that isn't updating LinkedIn?
turns.reply:
Morning-after embarrassment is real — the shame often shows up louder once the shock thins out. You do not have to turn today into a job hunt.

One thing that isn’t LinkedIn: step outside for ten minutes with no agenda — light, air, a short walk around the block. Or, if going out feels like too much, drink a full glass of water and open a window. Tiny body care counts as a real step when your nervous system is still catching up.

arcs.title: Invited brutal truth about stuckness
arcs.intent: When asked for hard honesty: clear + kind, not cruel

turns.user: I've been stuck for months. Be brutally honest with me — why isn't this getting better?
turns.reply:
You’ve been stuck for months — and asking for the hard version of why.

Here’s the blunt truth: it often doesn’t get better on its own because “stuck” isn’t laziness or a character flaw. It’s usually a loop — low energy/motivation, rumination, avoiding the hard things that would create movement, and waiting for motivation to show up first. Motivation usually follows action, not the other way around. Months of that loop can feel like proof you’re broken. It’s not proof. It’s a pattern that keeps reinforcing itself.

I can’t name *your* exact reason without more of your picture — sleep, isolation, grief, health, what you’ve already tried. Want the honest next cut: what’s been the main thing keeping the loop going for you?

turns.user: That was honest enough. Soften a little now — one gentle next step.
turns.reply:
Okay. Softer from here.

You’ve been stuck for months — that loop doesn’t have to get fixed all at once. One gentle next step: for the next two minutes, do one small body thing — water, stand by a window, or stretch your shoulders. Nothing bigger. When you’re ready, we can name what the loop has been feeding on.

arcs.title: Mission compound — seed → affirm → checkpoint → stall
arcs.intent: Persist mission; gate guidance; stall extends horizon

turns.user: What I really want over the next year is to feel steady enough to rebuild a life that isn't just surviving.
turns.reply:
What you’re naming is clear: over the next year, you want to feel **steady enough** to **rebuild** a life — not stay stuck in surviving. That matters. Surviving keeps you here; steadiness is what makes rebuilding feel possible instead of impossible.

I’m here with that. If you want, we can stay with what “steady enough” would even feel like for you — or what part of life you’re most hoping to rebuild when you have a little more ground under you.

turns.user: Yes — that is my mission. Track it with me.
turns.reply:
Yes — I’m tracking it with you.

Your mission for the next year: feel **steady enough** to **rebuild** a life that isn’t just surviving. I’ll hold that as the north star — no pressure to prove anything today. When you’re ready, we can name one small thing that helps you feel a little more steady, or just sit with the mission as it is.

turns.user: What's one small checkpoint that isn't overwhelming?
turns.reply:
One small checkpoint: name **one** way you can reach help if things get heavy — a person, a crisis line, or a place you’d go. You don’t have to use it today. Just knowing it’s there counts as staying within reach.

That’s a Safety-rung step toward “steady enough” — tiny, reversible, and enough for now. Want to pick that contact together, or name something even smaller for your body first (water, food, a short rest)?

turns.user: I couldn't do it. Back to square one. This is taking forever.
turns.reply:
Not square one — you’re still here, and that counts. Not being able to name a contact doesn’t erase the mission; it just means that step felt too big right now. “Taking forever” is information, not failure. Paths to “steady enough” often run longer than we want, and stuck isn’t a character flaw.

We can shrink it. Even smaller than a person or a line: just notice whether your body feels a little safer after water, a snack, or one slow breath. No pressure to finish anything. Want that tiny body check, or want to sit with the weight of “forever” for a minute first?
